en: Oṃ!
May there be prosperity for the venerable Jñānaprasūna, whose abode is the Lord.
Salutations to the Lord of Śrī-Kālahastīśvara;
they declare him to be the supreme destroyer of the marks of the heated discus, and the collection of the Vedas beginning with the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava.
One should praise Śiva, the non-dual Lord of all, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having meditated upon the venerable Śaṅkarācāryas, who bestow the nectar of non-duality, [this work] is for the joy of the virtuous,
which destroys the branding of the heated discus upon the body.

In this world, indeed, certain non-Vedic people, regarding the Pāñcarātra Āgama as authoritative, have— for the purpose of deluding the world—combined mantras recited in the direct Śrutis, such as "pavitraṃ te," with certain other mantras fabricated by that Āgama to be Vedic in nature; and on the basis of the meaning of those [fabricated] mantras, they believe that the rite of branding with the heated discus (taptacakrāṅkana) is established.

That water of a mirage is indeed fruitless for one who is thirsty; for instance, it is said in the tenth Anuvāka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka: "O Brahmanaspati, your purifier is spread out; you, the Lord, encompass its limbs on every side. One whose body has not been heated by austerity does not partake of that which is raw; those who carry it, having reached it, are consumed. Thus it is.

Thus it is said in the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "The foot is a wide-spreading, purifying vessel; purified by which one crosses over evil deeds. Purified by that pure, sanctifying [foot], may we cross over sin and overcome unrighteousness."

Likewise, in that very same place [it is said]: "May the radiant door of the world—the purifier, luminous, shining, and glorious, yielding many streams of immortality—grant us a footing in this world for our well-being."

Thus, in the Ṛgveda, in the seventh Aṣṭaka, in the fourth Adhyāya, in the eighth Varga: "Like a soaring hawk, far-reaching, the drop that finds the kine, bearing his weapons, surging toward the wave of the waters, the buffalo proclaims the ocean as his fourth abode."

Thus [it is said]. There are four mantras recited in the direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Among them, the mantra beginning with "That purifier... is used as follows: "The Udgātṛ priests, having established the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, spread a purifier (*pavitra*) over it with its fringes pointing north; the sacrificer consecrates the spreading purifier with the mantra, 'The purifier is spread for thee, O Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*)'. By this, it is enjoined for the consecration of the purifier while it is being spread. However, in the *Pāñcarātra*, a different application is seen for the installation of the discus (*cakra*), such as in the passage: "Then, during the installation, one should mutter the respective name-mantras," and so forth.

The mantra "caraṇaṃ pavitraṃ lokasya dvāram" (the foot is the purifier, the door of the world) is found in the *Kāṭhaka* [Saṃhitā] as the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* for the fifth oblation in the sacrifice named *Pāpman*, which consists of five parts, according to the rule: "In the fivefold [sacrifice], the foot is the fifth. One should not suspect that an action can lack the status of being a deity; for in the *Pārvaṇa-homa*, we see that the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices possess the status of deities, as in: "We worship the Bull, the vigorous, the Full Moon; may it yield for us excellent strength and thousandfold increase of wealth for our life and prosperity. Thus, the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices are seen to function as deities.

Here too, in the context of the fourfold sacrifice (*iṣṭi-catuṣṭaya*)—where it is seen that austerity (*tapas*) is the first deity, faith (*śraddhā*) the second, truth (*satya*) the third, and mind (*manas*) the fourth—the word *caraṇa* must be intended to mean "that which is to be performed," by virtue of its association with those [deities]. This is because in the fourth sacrifice, "the sky is the fourth," the *div* (sky) is seen to be the deity; and because in such passages as "O Sacrifice, homage to you, O Sacrifice! and "The Sacrifice is auspicious," the Sacrifice is seen to be the object of prayer and adoration.

Therefore, the ritual to be performed consists precisely of the *caraṇa-mantras*. The sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) dedicated to those deities is the *caraṇeṣṭi*. In that sacrifice, these two mantras are employed as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. In the *Pāñcarātra*, regarding the chapter on bathing and other rites: with the entire *Puruṣasūkta*, beginning with "śanaiḥ śanaiḥ," [the Lord] was placed in the Soma vessel with the mantra "caraṇaṃ pavitraṃ vitatam"; in the Rudra vessel with "lokasya dvāram arcimat"; on the right arm of the Brahmin positioned facing east with "dīkṣiṇe tu bhuje vipra"; and in the Agni vessel with "nicikṣepa suṣaṇam."

Having applied the *ūrdhva-puṇḍra* with the mantra while facing the southern direction, the Brāhmaṇa [should apply it] on his right arm with the mantra "yātudhānī-gatena vai. With the mantra "viṣṇunā taptamaśnanti," he applies it while facing the western direction. Then, at the time of installation, he should mutter the respective *jñāna-mantra* ending with "tatas sthāpana-kāle tu. At the time of installation, beginning with those words, he should cause the best of the twice-born to recite the mantra beginning with "vidyāṅgadām. Furthermore, he should cause the Bahvṛcas to recite the mantra beginning with "camūṣac chyenaḥ prateviṣṭaḥ. He should cause the Kaṭhas to recite the supreme mantra: "dhṛtordhva-puṇḍraḥ kṛta-cakraḥ."

The application of these mantras in the rites of bathing and installation is stated in sequence: "pavitraṃ te vitataṃ," "etat mantraṃ yajurmayaṃ," "kṣumāhuve," "sāmajñān," "pavitraṃ iti agniḥ," and "yebhir vayaṃ urukrama. By this [application], the use of these mantras is prescribed for the daily bathing and installation. Thus, by such statements as "at the time of installation, one should mutter the *saṃjñā-mantra*," it is enjoined that at the times of installation, one should indeed recite the mantras beginning with "pavitraṃ te."

Furthermore, the conclusion of the Mīmāṃsakas is that mantras employed in recitation (japa) are merely subordinate elements to the injunctions for specific rites, by way of manifesting the means and the deities of those rites which are to be performed. Consequently, the hope that an injunction for the branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*)—which is not the subject under discussion—is obtainable through a reflection on the meaning of such mantras, is mere wishful thinking.

Even upon a careful examination of the meaning, it is not possible for mantras such as "pavitraṃ te" and others to enjoin the practice of branding with the *cakra*; for instance, in the mantra "pavitraṃ te," the word *Brahmaṇaspati* has the sense of Prajāpati.

"One practicing exorcism should offer a victim with brown ears to Brāhmaṇaspati; he should prepare a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa before [the enemy's] departure. Having caused his rival to be seized by Varuṇa himself, he overcomes him through the Brāhmaṇa. It has brown ears—this, indeed, is the form of the Brāhmaṇa," so it is heard. "He overcomes him through the Brāhmaṇa; this, indeed, is the form of the Brāhmaṇa"—by means of this supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), the meaning of the word *Brāhmaṇaspati*, which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) in the term *brāhmaṇaspatyām*, is referred back.

One who desires a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Brāhmaṇaspati. Verily, he [Brāhmaṇaspati] favors him with his own portion; he [the deity] bestows kinsmen upon him, and he becomes possessed of a village. "The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses should contain the word 'group' (*gaṇa*)," it is said. There are two mantras—"O you, the lord of groups" (*gaṇānāṃ tvā*) and "with this company" (*sa ij janena*)—which are prescribed as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*.

In that context, regarding the *puronuvākyā* verse, "O Brahmaṇaspati, the eldest king of the Brahmas," the word "Brahmā" refers to the creator of the Vedas and the Brāhmaṇas; thus, it is determined that Brahman alone is the referent of the term *brahmaṇaspati*. Furthermore, in the *yājyā* verse, "He who desires to win over the father of the gods," he who is renowned as the creator of the gods and so forth—namely Brahman—is determined to be the referent of the term *brahmaṇaspati*. The word *pavitra* is derived from the sense of an instrument for purifying (*pavana*).

Therefore, the *prājāpatya* is a purifier (*pavitra*); gold is indeed a purifier; clarified butter (*ājya*) is indeed a purifier; the *darbha* grasses are indeed purifiers; "O you two purifiers belonging to Viṣṇu!"—"May Agni, the purifier, purify me!"—"May Soma, the purifier, purify me!"—and furthermore, "I shall hereafter proclaim all the purifiers of the Vedas; that which is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things"—in such passages, the function [of the word] is established even without postulating a difference in the primary denotative power (*śakti*) regarding multiple objects.

The fact that austerity (*tapas*) is a cause of heat is established by such scriptural passages as, "When his skin, bones, joints, flesh, and fat [are consumed]... and so forth, regarding the austerity that is an auxiliary to *śrauta* rites. Furthermore, even for the *smārta* rite of the installation of a ritual wheel (*cakrapratiṣṭhā*), which consists of observances (*niyama*) such as fasting and sleeping on the ground, there is indeed the quality of being a cause of heat. According to the conclusion of Mīmāṃsā, the purpose of mantras is solely the manifestation of one of the following: a deity, an action, or a means of accomplishing that action. Therefore, the meaning should be described in a way that is consistent with both types of application—*śrauta* and *smārta*—due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

And thus, this is the meaning: O Brahmanaspati, O Brahmā, you are the Lord; you encompass all limbs from every side—that is, you pervade all individual bodies by way of being their collective totality (samaṣṭi). That which belongs to you, which is pure as its very back, which is the means for the purification of Soma intended in the Śrauta ritual, or the cloth intended in the Smārta rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā), or the deity-form itself, or the form of the installation rite, or the form of the materials used for that rite—whatever is intended here as the cause of the sacrificer’s purification—that is what is meant.

It revolves, being spread out or pervaded by threads. Having performed this purifier, one whose body has not been heated—that is, whose body has not been refined—by the austerity connected with the rite in question; for that very reason, being raw, uncooked, and having not fulfilled his qualification, he does not enjoy the fruit of that rite in question. "Carrying this"—meaning they attain the fruit of that rite in question which is accomplished through the rite in question. And thus, because there is no meaning whatsoever conducive to the injunction for wearing the discus.

Let alone the accomplishment of the rite of wearing the disc (*cakradhāraṇa*) through this mantra; likewise, for mantras such as "The foot is pure" (*caraṇaṃ pavitram*), only a single meaning should be described that is consistent with both its Vedic and Smṛti applications. The "foot" refers to the prescribed ritual action—consisting of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice in the Vedic context and the bathing with the disc and other rites in the Smṛti context—and how is that action "pure"? It is purifying (*śodhaka*). For it is well known from the Smṛti, "By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil," that ritual actions possess the power to remove sin.

And because it is practiced by all people; or because the non-experience of the fruits of karma is universal; or because the Purāṇa is connected with the beginningless Veda; or because it is beginningless in its tradition—that by which one is purified: since it is universally accepted that obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) rites remove evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*), by that purifier, by that cleanser, being pure—since it is understood through the Veda which possesses intrinsic authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*)—may we, purified by that partless [Purāṇa], cross over evil and enmity.

Being rendered sinless by the performance of the prescribed rites, one does not experience the suffering that is the fruit of sin. It is the gateway to the world of heaven and serves as the means for attaining it; it is "flaming" (arcis-mat) because it is accomplished through fire. For this very reason, it is "luminous" (mahasvat), endowed with radiance or majesty, and "glorious" (jyotiṣmat), possessed of the attainable heaven.

In such passages as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; we have seen the light," the word *jyotis* (light) is used to denote heaven (*svarga*). Alternatively, because it is stated that "whatever one performs with knowledge becomes more powerful," *jyotiḥ* refers to action (*karman*) conjoined with knowledge. For this very reason, it is "shining" (*bhrājamānam*), meaning beautiful. Or else, what kind of "path" (*caraṇam*) is it? It is the "door of the world" (*lokasya dvāram*), because the door to heaven consists of light and because it is the abode of the deities; these epithets are thus applicable. Furthermore, it is not merely by defining the door of action that [the path is characterized].

"The gate of heaven is unbarred; happy are the kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a battle"—for thus, in the *Bhagavadgītā*, even the act of fighting is described as being the very gate of heaven. It yields a continuous stream of nectar produced from the churning of the ocean of immortality; or rather, it "milks" (*duhānam*) many streams (*dhārāḥ*)—that is, successions (*saṃtatīḥ*)—of the nectar of heavenly bliss, providing uninterrupted heavenly joys in manifold ways (*bahudhā*). And this is fitting, because of the existence of various kinds of pleasures in the heavenly world.

May he establish us—us who are situated well, that is, firmly established—in this world which is to be accomplished through the rites performed; namely, the rite in the form of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice prescribed by the Śruti, and the rite in the form of the bathing (*abhiṣeka*) prescribed by the Smṛti. If it is objected that in performing such a purpose there is no manifestation of a deity, we say no; for since the efficacy of the application (*viniyoga*) of mantras is stated to arise solely from their manifesting one of these: the deity, the ritual action, or the means of accomplishing that action, here the efficacy is possible precisely through the manifestation of the ritual action.

Furthermore, because it has been established here that the status of being a deity arises from action alone, it is impossible to claim that the injunction for branding with the heated discus is obtained through the power of the meaning of this mantra.

In this manner, the meaning of the mantra beginning with *evam̐ camūṣat* should also be described in accordance with its application (*viniyoga*) for the consecration of the wheel (*cakrābhiṣeka*). And that [meaning] is as follows: *śakunaḥ* means a hawk, a bird, namely Garuḍa. *Camūṣat* means he moves between heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*). Moving about is the natural disposition of birds, especially of Garuḍa, because his movement is unimpeded. *Govinduḥ* means the bearer of Viṣṇu; it is well known indeed that Garuḍa is the vehicle of Viṣṇu. Alternatively, in the word *govinduḥ*, the genitive case is used by way of transposition in the sense of the accusative, and *bibhrat* is the form ending in *-tvā*.

The meaning is that he is the vehicle of Govinda. *Drapsa* refers to a portion of Govinda; or else, it means one who exists in proximity to flowing water; or else, through his union with the wind, he is the Sun, according to the Vedic revelation: "That Āditya is the *drapsa*. Bearing weapons—here the word *āyudha* (weapon) is used without a prefix to denote his own weapon specifically—for the claws, beaks, and so forth of birds are weapons established by their very nature, yet for Garuḍa there are others as well. Bearing these, he holds them.

Alternatively, at the time of his departure, Viṣṇu—his own master—deposited his weapons within himself; bearing those, he proceeds. For those who set forth indeed place their weapons upon their own vehicles at the time of departure. And here, the very act of departure is described for the sake of the subsequent verse. Reaching the wave of the waters, that is, the ocean—the state of being "wavy" (ūrmitva) arising from its abundance of waves—he, reaching it, attains that which is the fourth abode, situated on the far shore of the ocean, known as Śvetadvīpa. He is the Great One (Mahiṣa), great by virtue of both his essential nature and his majesty; he reaches [that state], he attains it.

Because of the use of synonymous terms such as *juṣata* (he enjoys), the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*) is understood. Here, by the statement "being mixed with the ocean, he attains the fourth abode" (*dhāma*), it is understood that he goes above the ocean. Furthermore, by the phrase "Govinda supports [him]," it is understood that he arrives together with Govinda, who has mounted him, and with his own vehicle. By the phrase "the drop, being mixed with the wave," contact with water is understood. By the phrase "he attains the abode," his remaining in his own place is understood.

Thus, it is revealed that the consecration and installation of the discus of Govinda in its proper place is preceded by a connection consisting of the ritual bathing with water from jars resembling the waves of the ocean. This is because the function of a mantra is precisely to reveal the meaning of what is to be performed. It is not the case that the mantra primarily reveals only the consecration and installation of Govinda; rather, one must explain how the mantra accords with the revelation of the consecration and installation of the discus.

Since the suitability of the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, which are employed in the *cakrābhiṣeka*, has been stated by the proponents of the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) themselves in their *Saccaritrarakṣā*, it is possible that the same applies here as well.

Thus, when a meaning consistent with both applications is possible, the hope that an application inconsistent with them—characterized by defects such as the burden of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) or *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses)—might nevertheless result in an injunction for branding with a disc (*cakrāṅkana*) by the force of such a [forced] meaning, is far-fetched. For instance, regarding the mantra "pavitram te" (*The purifier is yours*), those who advocate for the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) describe its meaning as follows: "O Lord of Brahmā, O four-faced one, you are the master (*īśvara*) of Viṣṇu; you pervade (*paryeṣi*) all the limbs of everyone from every side."

The word "tava" (of you) refers to the pervasive Lord; one must supply the phrase "that wheel which exists as the spread-out purifier. By that heated wheel, those whose bodies are not heated (*ataptatanūḥ*)—that is, raw, uncooked, or rather, whose sins are unburnt—do not attain that well-known specific bliss characterized by liberation. Therefore, carrying the burning of the purifier, they are called "heated" (*tapta*), meaning fully matured; they "attain" (*samāśata*) that bliss, which means they reach it. Thus is the meaning.

The word *atrapavitra* must be assumed to denote the *cakra*; and on the basis of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the word *brahmaṇaspati*, which is conventionally derived as referring to a specific deity, must be assumed to have the unestablished meaning of Viṣṇu; the three words *yat asti tena* must be supplied as ellipsis; and in the phrase *ataptatanūḥ*, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be assumed for the word *tanū*, which denotes the entire body, to refer specifically to the armpits.

Therefore, by the word "that" (*tat*)—which refers back to the preceding phrase "one whose body is not scorched" (*ataptatanuḥ*) and denotes the wheel alone—the "wheel heated by fire" (*vahnitaptacakra*) must be indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Since the mere [word "wheel"] lacks the quality of being a cause of torment, the qualifying term "heated by fire" (*vahnitapta*) must either be supplied or understood. Furthermore, one must assume that the two instances of the word "that" refer to the happiness of liberation (*mokṣasukha*), which is not proximate [to the context]. Moreover, the meaning of the mantra must be stated in accordance with the specific ritual action for which it is employed.

This mantra is employed for the installation of the *cakra*; therefore, its significance must be explained either by revealing the four deities, by revealing the act of installation, or by revealing the means (*sādhana*) thereof. However, such [explanations] are not possible in the description of the meaning as stated by you. Rather, you are propounding that for a certain person there is no liberation in the absence of the burning of the arms, whereas there is liberation upon the burning of the arms; yet that meaning is indeed inconsistent with the ritual at hand (*prakṛtakarma*). Furthermore:

Since the description of a meaning intended for one’s own sake—which is consistent with both the Śruti and Smṛti—is corrupted by many stated defects and is therefore unreliable, the injunction to wear the discus (cakradhāraṇa) is not established by the force of the description of the meaning as propounded by others.

Furthermore, the injunction for wearing the discus (*cakra*) is not possible on the strength of the meaning of these two mantras: "The foot is the purifier" and "The door of the world. For instance, the proponents of the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) describe the meaning of those two mantras as follows: "By which foot [the Lord] is purified; by the marking with which [He] is purified; [by which] all evil deeds, all sins, He crosses over; that is spread out (*vitata*), extensive, ancient (*purāṇa*), eternal (*sanātana*), the foot."

By explaining the meaning of the word *cakraṃtha-caraṇa*, [it is shown that] because of the reading in the *Nighaṇṭu*—“the foot (*caraṇa*) is the discus (*cakra*), for it is pure”—the word *caraṇa* refers to the *Sudarśana* [discus]. It is "pure" (*pavitra*) because it wards off every sin belonging to those connected with it. Therefore, by that "pure" (*śuddhena*)—meaning inherently pure—and "purifying" (*pavitreṇa*)—meaning being the cause of purification even for those connected with it—foot, we are purified; that is, made clean by being marked with it. May we "cross over" (*atitarema*) evil; that is, may we exist having transcended the enemy (*arātiṃ*) who is of the nature of sin.

*Arcimat* (possessing rays), *jyotiṣmat* (possessing light), and *mahasvat* (possessing splendor)—there is no tautology here because the distinctions between flames, rays, and general radiance are intended. Since the Sudarśana [discus] is self-luminous, its state of being *arciṣmat* and so forth is appropriate either by virtue of its natural brilliance or its heat during the time of being worn. For this very reason, it is *bhrājamānam* (shining) and *pavitram* (pure), because it removes sin. It is "the door of the world" (*lokasya dvāram*) because it is the means to worlds such as heaven. It is "yielding the stream of immortality in many ways" (*amṛtasya dhārā bahudhā dohamānam*), because it is the means to liberation. It is "milking" (*duhānam*) through various means for the sake of experiencing liberation.

"May such a discus (cakra) place us—'naḥ' meaning 'us'—well-situated and well-established in this world; that is to say, by being the means for accomplishing all human goals (puruṣārtha), may it make us steady in the pursuit of those goals. Thus, from understanding the meaning that the discus existing on one's own body should act in this way, the injunction 'the mark of the discus should be branded' is inferred. This is the conviction of those who advocate for the heated seal (taptamudrā). To this, it is replied: [The following verse:]...

Regarding that, how is the word *caraṇa* in the two mantras derived in the sense of "branding with a disc" (*cakrāṅkana*)—is it by convention (*rūḍhi*), by etymology (*yoga*), or by metaphor (*lakṣaṇā*)? It cannot be the first, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that. Nor can it be the second, because there is no etymological derivation (*yoga*) suitable for the meaning of "disc. Nor should it be argued that the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) "the disc is the purifying foot" (*pavitraṃ caraṇaṃ cakraṃ*) is certain; for this is not seen in the Vedic glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), nor even in secular works on grammar and gender (*nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*).

The claim that the *caraṇa*, *cakra*, *lokadvāra*, and *sudarśana* are impure because they serve merely as conventional designations for the *Pañcarātra* system favored by [the opponent] is unfounded; for such lexicographical statements as "these—*cakra*, *paramātman*, and so forth—are synonyms" are merely fabricated. Otherwise, in the first mantra, the usage of "the pure *caraṇa*" would result in the synonym "by that pure [one]" (*tena pavitreṇa*), and in the second mantra, the usage of "the pure *caraṇa*, the door to the worlds" (*lokadvāraṃ pavitraṃ caraṇam*) would likewise result in the synonym "the pure door to the worlds."

For a wise person does not say "bring the pot-maker" when they ought to say "bring the pot. Furthermore, dictionaries do not possess the power to determine conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Even though the word *śukla* (white) is established in the dictionary as denoting a quality (*guṇa*), it is established by the Naiyāyikas that its primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the quality rather than the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), because the latter would involve a complexity in the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakagaurava*). They maintain that while the word has the power to denote the quality, its capacity to convey the possessor of the quality occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor should it be argued that denotative power is determined solely from the beginningless linguistic usage of elders; for such usage is not observed in certain cases.

For when an elder says to a youth, "Bring the Sudarśana," the youth understands by the words "Sudarśana" and "wheel" that very object which he knows the elder intends; likewise, even when told, "Bring the pavitra, look at the feet," he understands by the words "pavitra" and "feet" that very same object. On the contrary, he understands it as a specific substance intended to be a means of purification. Indeed, there is no Vedic etymological derivation (vyutpatti) here such as one finds in [the injunctions] "he hews the sacrificial post" (yūpaṃ takṣati) or "he offers in the Āhavanīya fire" (āhavanīye juhoti).

Therefore, the suffix *itra* cannot apply to the words *pavitra* and *caraṇa*. Now, it might be argued that in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the word *pavitra* is established as being used in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For instance, there is a Pāṇinian rule: "After the roots *ṛ*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *kan*, *san*, *car*, and *ha*, the suffix *itra* is applied. This yields *aritram*, *lavitram*, *dhavitram*, *savitram*, *khanitram*, *sahitram*, and *caritram*. Regarding the word *pavitra*: from the root *pū*, the suffix *itra* is applied when a name is to be formed, resulting in *pavitra*. It refers to that by which clarified butter (*ājya*) is purified, and also to the ring of grass used for binding the sacrificial ladle. Furthermore, there is a rule: "The suffix *itra* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when referring to a Ṛṣi or a deity."

In the rule "pūyate 'nena" (it is purified by this), the suffix *itra* occurs when the sense is that of an instrument (*karaṇa*), a deity (*devatā*), or an agent (*kartṛ*). An *ṛṣi* is a Vedic mantra; it is called *pavitra* because "one is purified by means of it. Regarding the deity, however, Agni is the *pavitragama*, as in the formula "may he purify [us]. If it is argued that the word *pavitra* should thus be a designation (*saṃjñā*) for the ring-finger (*anāmikā*)—which is the means of straining the clarified butter (*ājya*)—and also for the deity, then [we reply]: if that were so, since the term would already be established by the rule on technical names (*saṃjñā-sūtra*) alone, the formulation of the specific rule "when the sense is that of an agent, an *ṛṣi*, or a deity" would be redundant.

Therefore, since the names of the means of purification (*pavitrana*) and the finger-wrappings (*aṅguliveṣṭana*) are fixed as designations, the status of the names for the wheels and deities is not established. If it is argued: "But surely, even if the words *pavitra* and *caraṇa* do not denote the wheels, their status as names is understood from the *Pāñcarātra-āgama* statement, 'At the time of their installation, one should mutter the respective name-mantras,' because it is understood that the mantras employed in the rite of installation possess the nature of names"—we reply: this is not so, [as the passage] beginning with "vidyāṅgadām" [refers to something else].

This is because other mantras are also prescribed by the passage beginning with "He should cause the best of the twice-born to recite this," and because the words "discus" (*cakra*) and so forth are absent therein; furthermore, they are absent in the *Śākuna-sūkta*. As for the fact that some mantras such as "He has entered the lotus-discus" (*prati viṣṭo abja-cakre*) contain a connection to these names, that alone is sufficient to justify their status as "name-mantras" (*saṃjñā-mantra*), just as in the case of the statement "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi* bricks. Or, even if that connection exists through a figurative name, since there is an injunction for these mantras to be merely recited (*japya*), there is no intention to convey their literal meaning. Otherwise...

"O Agni, I prepare for you a pleasant seat; with a stream of ghee, I fashion it as a most auspicious resting place. Upon that immortal [seat], do thou, being well-disposed, take thy stand"—from such mantras as these, it would follow that insentient objects like the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) possess sentient attributes such as being "well-disposed."

Nor should it be argued that because the Puruṣasutra mentions the conscious attributes of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)—such as when they did not see the cake, which was a tortoise moving about as a living being, they said, "O Indra, crawl forth"—therefore the qualities of being well-disposed and so on are also possible for the cake. This is because that passage is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the injunction, "The cake for Agni, prepared on eight potsherds, becomes excluded on the new moon and full moon days," and thus lacks an independent purport regarding its own literal meaning; consequently, the crawling of the cake is not established by such a statement.

Otherwise, it would result in the inconsistency of establishing the authority of the statement, "The gods did not discern the directions when they settled upon the sacrificial ground for the gods," as being merely a commendatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) of the injunction regarding the sacrificial ground. Nor should it be argued that there is no logical impossibility here—just as the possession of bodies and other attributes by the gods is established through *arthavādas* such as "the thunderbolt-wielder, the destroyer of cities"—because in this case, the movement of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-prasarpaṇa*) is not established due to its contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*). Otherwise, [it would follow that] "his head fell off as his bowstring snapped."

From such statements as "When [the head] fell with the sound 'Ghrām'," the falling of the head of Viṣṇu—who is the form of the sacrifice—is established; and from the statement beginning with "Sāra," the weeping of Rudra—the Lord of the Sacrifice—is likewise established. Nor should it be asked how Viṣṇu possesses the nature of the sacrifice or how Rudra possesses lordship over the sacrifice, for this is beyond dispute due to its being well-known from the Śruti: "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice" and "The waters [brought] King Rudra to the Adhvara."

Therefore, the claim that a different meaning is established through an *arthavāda* which has become an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of an injunction is to be rejected. Consequently, the idea that mantras possess injunctive power by virtue of an *arthavāda* is utterly discarded. Nor should it be argued that, because of the statement in the *Pāñcarātra Āgama*—"The Sudarśana [is seen] thus by those who have seen the Sudarśana"—it is necessary that these two [mantras] refer to the Sudarśana. For [the same text states]: "The foot, the purifier, the extended" refers to Soma; "The radiant gate of the world" refers to Rudra. And by these eight mantras, as well as others related to the Sudarśana... [the respective deities are indicated].

This is because the term *saudarśana* is intended to refer specifically to those [mantras] distinct from the mantra beginning with "itīcaraṇaṃ pavitram," and because it is logical for the *Puruṣasūkta* and others to be designated as *saudarśana* due to their connection with the ritual bathing (*snapana*) of the Sudarśana [discus], just as in the case of other such texts.

As for the claim that the word *caraṇa* in the compound *yatturathacaraṇa* refers to the Sudarśana discus through the use of a partial expression (*ardhokti*), that too is incorrect. It is improper to assume a partial expression when it is possible to do so; rather, it is more logical to assume that the word *caraṇa* here is a partial expression for "Viṣṇu’s feet. This is because the word *caraṇa* by itself is well-known to mean "foot," and because this interpretation accords with the overall meaning of the mantra. Nor should it be argued that such an assumption is made out of deference to the specific application (*viniyoga*) in the present context; for since these two mantras are applied to the bathing of the discus (*cakrasnapana*), their utility is established simply by expressing the meanings well-known in common usage, making any strained interpretation unjustified.

Nor should it be argued that the word *pavitra* has the meaning of "disc" (*cakra*) on the basis of the mantra cited from the Sāmaveda beginning with "nacapavitramityagniḥ," because, having introduced the topic with "At the time of installation, one should mutter the respective mantra for each [deity]," the *Pāñcarātra* states the application of this mantra at the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) with the words "the Sāman-mantras such as *kṣumāhava* and also *pavitraṃ agniḥ*. It is not possible to determine the Vedic status of a text based solely on a citation from the *Pāñcarātra*.

Nevertheless, because there is no intention to express the literal meaning of the mantras employed for recitation (*japa*), and because [the mantra] serves merely as a subordinate part of the ritual procedure for the consecration of the *cakra* by means of manifesting the *cakra* in some manner or other, the status of the word "panitra" as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the *cakra* is not established by this mantra. Otherwise, one would have to accept that the word "water" (*ap*) denotes everything on the basis of the mantra "All this was indeed water," or that the word "Brahman" is the technical name for all deities based on the statement "The Brahmin is indeed all the deities."

By the statement "Agni is all the deities," the word *agni* would indeed have the meaning of "all deities"; therefore, neither the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *pavitra* nor the injunction for the branding with the discus (*cakrāṅkana*) can be established through that mantra. Consequently, the word *pavitra* cannot denote the discus either by etymological derivation (*yoga*) or by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Nor is it the third [alternative]. For there is no lack of logical consistency (*anupapatti*). Indeed, if the words *caraṇa* and *pavitra* did not mean "discus," there would be no syntactic inconsistency (*vākyānupapatti*) in saying "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), nor would there be any inconsistency regarding the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*).

The purpose of a mantra lies in the manifestation of any one of the following: the deity, the ritual action, or the means of accomplishing that action. Since such a meaning can be established through the primary mode of signification (*mukhyavṛtti*) itself according to the method described above, it is impossible to assume a secondary mode of signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, since the consistency between Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smṛti-based (*smārta*) applications is maintained only through a single unified meaning, it is improper to assume an unestablished and divergent meaning.

It should not be argued that the word *caraṇa* (conduct) having the sense of "action" (*karman*) is likewise unknown; for this is established by the two sūtras: "If it be said that [the word] 'conduct' (*caraṇa*) [is meant], we say no, because it is used as an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*), so says Kārṣṇājini; but Bādari says it refers to good and evil deeds themselves (*sukṛta-duṣkṛte eva*)," and because the meaning of the word *caraṇa* as "action" has been determined in these and other texts such as their commentaries, specifically in the passage: "Those here whose conduct (*caraṇa*) is pleasant attain a pleasant womb; those whose conduct is foul attain a foul womb."

Furthermore, because in such applications as "The Vedas purify one who is devoid of conduct," it is extremely clear that [the word *pavitra*] has the sense of an action (*karman*). Moreover, the interpretation of the phrase "purified by which" as meaning "purified by its marking" is improper; for neither from the words nor from the context is either marking (*aṅkana*) or wearing (*dhāraṇa*) perceived here. Even the explanation of the meaning as "pure, purifying, and removing all sins through its own connection" is inconsistent; for although the quality of removing sin is obtained for "conduct" (*caraṇa*) by virtue of the word "pure" (*pavitra*), the specific sense of "through its own connection" is not perceived.

Because no inherent connection with the *pavitra* (purifier) is perceived, the claim that "they are purified by that *caraṇa* [foot] and rendered pure by its marking" is also inconsistent; for the word *caraṇa* does not convey the meaning of "marking. As for the argument that the three qualifiers in the second mantra—*arciṣmat*, *jyotiṣmat*, and *mahasvat*—are appropriate because of the heat during the state of wearing [the ring], that too is inconsistent; for the state of wearing is not conveyed by the mantra, nor is heat perceived from the meaning of the words.

For those who perform [the ritual] do not burn their arms with a wheel that possesses flames, light, and radiance; for if it were so, an undesirable consequence would arise due to excessive burning. Nor is this meaning conducive to the application of the rite of bathing (*snāna*); at the time of bathing, the wheel endowed with a divine form is not heated. Therefore, there are neither flames nor lights therein. Furthermore, by the phrase "the door to the worlds," its status as a means to heaven has been stated.

That too is inconsistent, because the status of being a means to heaven is well-established for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, whereas the wearing of the *cakra* is not accepted as a means to heaven. As for what was said—that "streams of immortality" refers to the experience of liberation—that too is incorrect. By its very nature, the word "streams of immortality" is understood to mean a continuous flow of happiness; it is improper to abandon that meaning and take it to mean the experience [of liberation], since liberation is not achieved through many diverse means.

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "There is no other path for going," and because it is impossible for there to be multiplicity or multiple streams [of liberation] given that the bliss of liberation is eternal, unitary, and singular; furthermore, the interpretation that "in this world, may he establish us on a firm foundation" is also inconsistent, since the wearer himself accepts that the wearing of the discus is not a means to liberation. Therefore, this meaning is not acceptable. Regarding the mantra *camūṣat*, those who advocate for the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) describe its meaning as follows: *drapsam* means like a drop, that is, minute or subtle; *camūṣat*.

Moving about and dwelling upon the alternating cycles of heaven and earth by the power of karma; a hawk—a bird so called because, like a hawk, it is capable of lifting itself up and is able to reach its own self; a sustainer, capable of supporting even those connected to him; a finder of cattle (*govindu*); one who has entered into the waters; bearing weapons; crossing over and traversing the wave of the waters, the ocean; most mighty and worthy of honor; the fourth station, the supreme place; he proclaims himself as the Bull (*ṛṣabha*).

Regarding this, the proponents of the *taptamudrā* (heated seal) hold the following view: because it has been stated that the attainment of the supreme station occurs only through the wearing of the discus (*cakradhāraṇa*), the injunction for the wearing of the discus is obtained from the phrase "wearing weapons" (*āyudhāni bibhrat*) used here by Govinda. Furthermore, they argue that the use of the words *śakuni* (bird) and *śyena* (hawk)—which denote a bird in general and a specific type of bird respectively—in the sense of "human" is not inconsistent; nor can it be said that such a meaning was expressed because no other way [of interpretation] exists, since it is possible to describe the meaning in the manner already stated without abandoning the conventional (*rūḍhi*) sense of the words.

Since the word *bibhrat* can be construed with the proximate word *govindaḥ*, it is improper to supply an ellipsis such as "capable of supporting even his own kinsmen" and thereby interpret the meaning. Nor should it be argued that such an interpretation is assumed for the sake of consistency with the present application (*viniyoga*); for even if one assumes such a thing according to the maxim "the disease is cured by eating garlic," consistency with the application is still not established.

It should not be argued that there is consistency with the context because the *sudarśana* [discus] is revealed as being connected to the action at hand by the statement, "bearing the weapons of Govinda. For if the revelation of the discus were intended merely to show that some man—unconnected to the action at hand—is bearing the weapon of the discus, it would be subordinate to that [mere description], and thus it would be useless for the action at hand, which consists of the bathing of the discus. Therefore, the phrase "nacagoviṃdurāyudhāni" does not describe the intended meaning, such as the heating [of the discus] in the ocean and so forth.

Thus, when a single meaning is possible that is consistent with the application (*viniyoga*) of both [texts], the postulation of a strained meaning inconsistent with that application—done merely for the sake of fulfilling one's own desires—is certainly to be disregarded by those who follow authoritative sources (*prāmāṇika*). If it is argued: "Nevertheless, since the mantras beginning with *cakram bibharti* are stated in the Pāñcarātra Āgama to have been recited in all Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the injunction for wearing the discus (*cakradhāraṇa-vidhi*) is established by the force of their meaning," we say: no.

Since the Lord Vyāsa himself established the lack of authority of the Pāñcarātra Āgama on the grounds of its contradiction with the Vedas through such sūtras as *Utpattyasaṃbhava*, it is impossible to determine with certainty that the mantras employed therein originate from direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Otherwise, one could just as easily establish that even the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such doctrines are supported by the authority of all the Vedic branches (*akhila-śākhā-pramāṇaka*); consequently, the establishment of the Pāñcarātra Āgama’s lack of authority by Vyāsa and others in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā would result in inconsistency.

Furthermore, this is because it would result in the untenability of establishing that the *Pāñcarātra* and other such systems lack Vedic authority within the *Dharmaśāstras*. To illustrate: in the *Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa* of Hemādri, Marīci states: "A *kuṇḍa*, a *golaka*, one who officiates for those unworthy of sacrifice (*ayājya-yājaka*), one whose body is marked with the discus (*cakrāṅkita-tanu*), as well as one marked with the *liṅga*, a slanderer (*dūṣaka*), a madman, and likewise a gambler—by these, the row of men is always defiled by sin. A Brahmin who eats the food of these [persons] shall incur only sin."

O King, one who eats at a single location should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Regarding this very point, the Vāmana Purāṇa states: "If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should heat the fire with his hand-seal (mudrā), he is not worthy of performing rituals here; he is indeed designated as a eunuch. Also in that same Nārada Purāṇa: "Since the body of a Brāhmaṇa consists of all the gods, what shall I say of that ignorant sinner by whom it has been heated? O King, wherever a person whose body is marked with the discus (cakra) or even marked with the linga recites the Puruṣasūkta, otherwise he shall go to the Raurava hell."

In that very *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "If a person, having heated the conch and discus, has them burn upon his body while still alive, he is a corpse even while living; he should be abandoned and excluded from all religious rites. In that same [work], the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "He who has no entitlement to receive a share in the Vedas or sacrifices—having heated the discus and other [emblems]—should wear them on both arms. If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should wear fire-rings (fire-stamped rings), one should look at the sun merely by the sight of him. In that same [work], the *Vahni Purāṇa*:

Having separately burnt the body of an elder brother with the conch, discus, and other [emblems], there is no atonement for this through bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth. An atonement for that has been declared by Pārāśarya: having shaved the hair, one should then perform the rite again, beginning with *garbhādhāna* (the rite of conception) and so on from the womb-vessel; thus the expiation consisting of sixfold repetitions of *kṛcchra* penances is proclaimed. In that very same *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Where one who is not an elder brother burns [the body] out of devotion, having [placed it] in the mouth... [and so on].

For it has been stated that expiation must be prescribed for those who enter the row of Brahmins marked with the heated seal (*taptamudrā*), who eat their food, dine together with them, look upon them, or accept gifts from them; this is established by the citations from the *Marīci-smṛti*, *Vāmana-purāṇa*, *Nārada-purāṇa*, *Liṅga-purāṇa*, *Āditya-purāṇa*, *Vahni-purāṇa*, *Kūrma-purāṇa*, and other sources, as well as by the authors of legal digests (*nibandhana*) such as Hemādri, who cite such texts as: "Having taken only a small amount of gold, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance; having performed half of that again, one should fast for one day," and so forth.

Because of the prescription of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) characterized by sixty-four *kṛcchras*—preceded by purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāras*) such as the *garbhādhāna* and others—for those who have made marks with heated metal, it is established that the wearing of the discus (*cakradhāraṇa*) is non-Vedic, and that the *Pāñcarātra Āgamas* and other texts prescribing it are intended for those outside the Vedic fold. Furthermore, in the *Viṣṇusmṛti* attributed to Vaidyanātha: "The marking with the conch, discus, and so forth, as well as dancing, singing, and the like, is a duty for the once-born (*ekajāti*) alone; it is not for the twice-born (*dvijāti*) under any circumstances."

That twice-born man whose body is marked with signs such as the heated conch and other emblems is a partaker of all torments and becomes a Caṇḍāla for ten million births. Likewise, one whose body is marked with the discus or marked with the liṅga is to be known as ineligible for the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis. Gobhila also says: "A Brāhmaṇa performing Śrauta and Smārta rites should not mark his limbs with emblems, even if they are connected to Viṣṇu and the like; whether heated or otherwise, he would become an outcast. Whether through ignorance, greed, or passion, [one who marks himself with] the Sudarśana..."

Seeing one who destroys his lineage, he should enter the water along with him; even one who possesses knowledge of the Vedas and the sacred fires, if he should draw the Sudarśana on the surface of his arm with water alone, he too destroys his family unto the seventh generation. That fool who bears the conch, the discus, and the lotus upon his body should be known as a heretic (pāṣaṇḍa), excluded from all religious rites. Śātātapa says: A Brāhmaṇa should not mark his limbs with the emblems of divine weapons; if he should mark them out of delusion, he falls [from his caste] without a doubt. Manu says:

One should not mark nor burn [the body] with the emblems of divine weapons; by burning or by marking, a Brahmin incurs degradation at that very moment. Bodhāyana says: One should not mark nor burn the body; if one burns it out of personal desire, he whose limbs have been burnt is no longer entitled to perform rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. In the Cakropaniṣad: Therefore, one should wear the conch and discus only on the bodies of Śūdras. In the Smṛtiratna: A Brahmin who, being of deluded intellect, makes a mark with heated seals, shall become a Śūdra in this life and a dog after death.

In another Smṛti: "He who makes a conch or a discus out of clay or heated iron shall be excluded like a Śūdra from all the duties of the twice-born. Just as wood grown in a cremation ground is unfit for all rites, so too a Brāhmaṇa marked with a discus is unfit for all rites. In the Brāhma Purāṇa: "The branding of heated seals was ordained by Hari for the lowest castes (antyajas) in ancient times; those whose palms are smeared with red sandalwood paste are indeed of the lowest castes. In the Mānava [Smṛti]: "One should never burn [the body] with weapons such as the conch or the discus."

The king should immediately banish those whose limbs have been burnt by fire. For branding is ordained for men who have fallen [from their status] due to some calamity; it is not prescribed for those who are pure, nor should one brand those who are already pure. One who is branded is disqualified from teaching and studying, from performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, from conversation, and from social association. In the Nāradīya: "The body of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as the refuge of all the gods. O King, if that [body] is scorched, what can I say of such a great sinner? That man who, being free from disease, burns his body without cause..."

Having extensively refuted the branding with the heated disc among Vedic practitioners by means of Smṛti statements spoken by Viṣṇu, Gobhila, Śātātapa, Manu, Bodhāyana, and others—such as "One should abandon him at offerings of *havya* and *kavya*, just as one abandons an outcaste"—as well as by Purāṇic statements from the Brahma, Mānava, Kūrma, Nārada, and other Purāṇas, [the author says]: "The single-minded devotees (*ekāntinaḥ*), O highly blessed one, who know my true nature and are stainless, should apply sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*) of the shape of my foot, leaving a space between them."

By such statements as these, the author establishes that the scriptural injunctions of the *Āgama* texts like the *Pāñcarātra*, which prescribe the wearing of the conch and discus (*śaṅkhacakradhāraṇa*), are intended for those who possess the specific qualification (*adhikāra*) for Tantra. He then cites them as authoritative evidence in that regard: "The Veda and all the Smṛtis and other texts rooted in the Veda are self-evident for mortals on this earth; yet there are others everywhere. O ascetics rich in penance, whatever path is contrary to the Veda is not the truth. However, for living beings who have strayed from the Vedic path, paths such as the *Pāñcarātra* become beneficial through the course of time."

"O twice-born ones, O best of sages, the marking with the conch, discus, and mace is not for other embodied beings; rather, for men who have been initiated into the Tantras, such marking is declared to be beneficial in due order. However, it is an obstacle for those who walk solely upon the path of the Vedas. These and other statements from the Skanda Purāṇa and other texts have been cited here. "A man who has fallen away from the Śruti and who fears the expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) prescribed by the Smṛtis should resort to the Tantra in order to gradually achieve the realization of the Śruti. Furthermore, the Tantras are protectors, in their proper sequence, of those who are established in the Tantras."
"Those who follow exclusively the Vedic path are free from obstacles"—thus have the qualified practitioners of the Tantras been described by Parāśara and others.

In this regard, since the cited statement from the *Śātātapa-smṛti* establishes that branding with a heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*) is a cause for loss of caste (*pātitya*), it is proven that the *Śātāpa-śruti* cited by the proponents of the heated seal (*taptamudrāvādin*) is fabricated. Furthermore, since the cited statement from *Parāśara* establishes that only one who has strayed from the Vedic path is eligible for the Tantras, the claim of the proponents of the heated seal—that the marking with a discus is enjoined in the latter section (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) of the *Parāśara-smṛti*—is to be rejected as baseless. Moreover, [this is so] according to Mādhavācārya, the commentator on the *Parāśara-smṛti*.

Since the *Anukramaṇikā-grantha* has already stated the extent of the Smṛtis, the number of *kāṇḍas*, the number of chapters (*adhyāyas*), and their respective subject matters (*prameya*), the subsequent section (*uttara-khaṇḍa*) is as non-existent as a hare's horn; furthermore, because it is tainted by the suspicion of being an interpolation, modern scholars are unable to determine the authority of those Smṛti and Purāṇa passages that were not cited by the authors of the original treatises. For this very reason, moderns employ Vedic mantras only in the manner determined by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*.

However, an application [of a scriptural injunction] cannot be postulated according to one's own intellect. Even in the performance of the meaning of a Smṛti, practitioners follow the very method determined by the great authors of digests (Nibandhakāras). It is not possible to consult the original Smṛti and then conduct oneself by imagining a meaning according to one's own intellect.

Therefore, since Hemādri, Vaidyanātha, and others have established in their Dharmaśāstra digests that the rule for branding with marks (cakrāṅkana) pertains to those outside the Veda who are qualified for Tantra, the Vedic character of such branding is not proven.

"He bears upon his body the discus that scorches the army of the gods; he is Viṣṇu, whom the self-controlled ascetics, free from passion, enter after shaking off their sins"—thus says a mantra from the Atharvaveda. "He cast down the Sudarśana, which was being shattered; he placed it between his arms. This immense splendor of Viṣṇu overcomes [all] by day and night; those people who would seek to defy it [perish]"—thus says a mantra from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka.

"O Viṣṇu, for the sake of crossing over birth and death, the lords of men take up the lotus, the discus, and the purifier (the conch) at their shoulders; others, the ancient ones, place Your marks upon their limbs. Thus, by the mantra found in the Puṣkala-saṃhitā of the Ṛgveda. "The high-souled one who, having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and bearing the discus, meditates on Viṣṇu—the Supreme, who dwells eternally in the heart, who is higher than the highest, greater than the great—by means of the sound of the mantra. Thus, by the mantra found in the Kaṭhavallī.

"A Brahmin should bear the *Sudarśana* on his right arm, and he should bear the conch (*śaṅkha*) on his left"—thus do those who know Brahman understand. This is according to the mantra found in the *Brahmasūkta* of the *Mahopaniṣad*. If it is argued that the rule for marking with the discus and conch is not obtained from the mantra "May we, marked by these signs of the Wide-strider (*Urukrama*), become fortunate in the world; those who go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu are thus marked"—which is found in the *Atharvaveda*—then [we reply]: no.

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the mantra "anuṣaṇaṃ bhidyamānam" is not present, because it is not found there. Even the Puṣkala-saṃhitā does not exist within the Ṛgveda, as it is not seen in the enumeration of its recensions (śākhās). The mantra "ṛtordhvapuṇḍra" is not found in the Kaṭha school, as it is not observed therein. Indeed, it is not possible for Vaidikas to determine the Vedanity of mantras whose application and essential nature are known solely through the Pāñcarātra Āgamas, by citing such examples.

Even if that were the case, the meaning must be described solely in accordance with their specific application (*viniyoga*), and not otherwise. Consequently, it has been stated [in the scriptures] that "at the time of bathing [the deity], one should mutter the respective names," and so forth; thus, the application of these mentioned mantras is declared for the consecration of the hand and for the bathing of the deity. The purpose of mantras is exclusively the manifestation of either the ritual action, its means, or its presiding deity; there is no other.

Therefore, since [the mantras] are subsidiary only to the rites of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth for the *cakra* under discussion—by way of illuminating that [consecration]—it follows that the rite of branding with the heated *cakra* (*taptacakrāṅkana*), which is not under discussion, cannot be established by those stated mantras. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that mantras such as "iṣe tvā," which are employed for acts like cutting branches, would establish the rite of eating, because they illuminate food and the like. If you accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), then since eating is also Vedic, those who abandon it would incur penance (*prāyaścitta*), just like those who abandon the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*).

Nor should it be argued that while there is no injunction regarding food because it is already established by natural desire (*rāga*), an injunction is possible here [regarding branding]; for even in this case, since a penance characterized by six years of *kṛcchra* penance preceded by re-initiation (*saṃskāra*) is prescribed for those who perform the branding with the heated discus, and since Āpastamba’s statement—"By the Śrutis, penance is ordained for a transgression of an injunction"—makes it known that penance has its cause in the transgression of an injunction, the status of branding as a transgression of an injunction cannot be established without an injunction prohibiting such branding.

Since this prohibition is understood as being internal [to the ritual], an injunction cannot be inferred by means of the mantras; otherwise, there would result the injunction of external animal slaughter through the mantras such as "O divine immolators," which are auxiliary to the immolation of the sacrificial animal in the Yoga sacrifice, because the prescription of expiation is equal in both cases. Nor can it be argued that such a thing does not occur there because of the existence of the direct prohibition, "One shall not kill."

In this regard, it should not be argued that the injunction is established because the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only for the Śūdra" indicates the perception of a prohibition against those other than Śūdras. This is because such an argument would contradict the established conclusion in the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*, where it was determined that even though injunctive suffixes exist in mantras such as "one should sacrifice three *kapiñjala* birds to Vasanta," they do not possess injunctive force.

Therefore, these aforementioned mantras serve only as supplements to the injunction for the consecration of the discus (*cakrapratiṣṭhā-vidhi*) by means of manifesting the deity of the discus; thus, there is no establishment of an injunction for branding with a heated discus for one who has not previously undergone the primary rite.

If it is asked, "Even so, how can the aforementioned scriptural passages have a meaning consistent with the ritual for the installation of the *cakra* (discus) as taught in the *Pāñcarātra*?"—the answer is as follows: The mantra beginning with "He who bears the *cakra*" (*cakram bibharti*) refers to one who, by means of his own body (*vapuṣā svarūpeṇa*), bears the *cakra* belonging to the immeasurable (*amitasya*), all-pervading (*sarvavyāptasya*) Viṣṇu—a *cakra* that is heated (*abhitaptam*) and blazing (*pradīptam*), the strength (*balam*) of the gods, and the cause of protection (*rakṣaṇahetubhūtam*). He who, preceded by the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) involving consecration in a water-jar (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), worships it with ritual offerings (*upacāraiḥ*), nourishes it, and gratifies it.

Shaking off evil, he goes to—that is, reaches—the world of Viṣṇu, which is the fruit of the act of installation, where those who are free from passion (yatayaḥ) enter. Thus, since a meaning consistent with the application of the ritual at hand is possible—namely, that any person whatsoever bears the heated disc upon his own body—he reaches the world of Viṣṇu by wearing the disc; any interpretation inconsistent with the application of the installation-rite at hand, such as the wearing of a heated seal (taptamudrā), is simply unacceptable.

Thus he cast down the "suṣaṇam" mantra; he placed—that is, he held—the Sudarśana in the middle of his arms, between his two arms. It was "bhidyamānam," meaning being divided in many ways, or variously; or alternatively, it means cutting through enemy hosts (the accusative usage is Vedic). He cast it down—that is, he hurled it—far away as "suṣaṇam," which causes the end of evil. Because it is "bhūridam," yielding abundant fruit, this is "vaiṣṇavam," belonging to Viṣṇu.

This Sudarśana possesses abundant splendor and overcomes the power of many enemies; it crushes and subdues them, and thus the meaning is that it destroys the heap of evil. Therefore, "people" (janāsaḥ) should always wear it by day and by night. Thus, the interpretation offered by the proponents of the *taptamudrā* (heated seal) is indeed unacceptable, because it is inconsistent with the specific application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra in its original context. The meaning consistent with the original application is as follows: Viṣṇu placed the beautiful Sudarśana, which brings great fortune and is the end-maker of enemies, upon his arm.

And at that time, it was being split apart; it is deposited as having a form corresponding to the destruction of enemies—that which he hurled and employed against his foes. That which is employed is "bhūridam," meaning it bestows much, possessing vast splendor. It overcomes and subdues the extensive power of many enemies. This is "vaiṣṇavam," belonging to Viṣṇu. O people (*janāsaḥ*), may you bear and cherish that Sudarśana both by day and by night—meaning during the two times of evening and morning. Bearing (*bibhṛyuḥ*) and cherishing (*puṣṇīyuḥ*) are synonymous terms.

The verbal root *ḍubhṛñ* signifies "to support" and "to nourish. Its application is seen in the verse: "He who has acquired knowledge from his brother should provide for that brother's family; therefore, even if he is unlearned, he shall receive a share of the wealth derived from that knowledge. Furthermore, it is stated: "And they should provide for her [the wife] until the end of her livelihood. This very act of nourishing, which is synonymous with supporting, is called "worship" (*pūjana*) when directed toward venerable persons. For this reason, there is a traditional saying among ritualists (*yājñika*) that "in a sacrifice, one must perform the selection and the supporting of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)."

In this context, "support" (*bharaṇa*) refers precisely to worship with garments, ornaments, and so forth. Accordingly, it has been explained by the authors of the treatises that regarding the statement, "One should worship [the deity] preceded by consecration and installation, both morning and evening, and likewise guests and servants; the husband and wife shall eat the remnants," the term "servants" (*bhṛtyāḥ*) refers to those who are to be supported, such as parents and others. Thus, since the meaning must be accepted as that which accords with the established tradition (*cakra-pratiṣṭhā*), any interpretation inconsistent with that—such as the practice of wearing heated metal seals (*taptamudrā*) and the like—is certainly not to be accepted.

If it is argued that even according to the method prescribed for those who wear heated seals (*nanu-tapta-mudrā*), there is some manner in which the manifestation of the discus (*cakra*) exists, and thus that too is consistent with the present context—this is not so. For one who bears the *Sudarśana* on his upper arm casts away sin; indeed, the Vaiṣṇava *Sudarśana* demonstrates its power over a multitude of enemies and thereby destroys the heap of sins. Therefore, by the implication of the statement "people should always bear it by day and night," it is said that the *Sudarśana* must be worn at all times for the purpose of destroying sin.

This being the case, how can any man whatsoever who is not connected with the subject at hand obtain a connection with the injunction regarding the wearing of the wheel (*cakradhāraṇa*), since that would be an acquisition of an injunction for something irrelevant? It cannot be said that the mere manifestation of the wheel possesses a connection with the subject at hand; for the manifestation of it does not serve the purpose of the subject matter, as it is merely conducive to the injunction for wearing it. Therefore, the position of those who advocate the wearing of heated seals (*taptamudrā*) is simply unacceptable.

In this manner, even the meaning of the mantra "evaṃprate viṣṇo abja-cakre" must be described in accordance with its application to the present ritual act: O Viṣṇu! Certain leaders of people (*śarṣaṇīndrāḥ*), who are wise (*jñāninaḥ*), in order to cross the ocean of birth (*janmāmbhodhim tartave*), at the time of the installation of Your image, place upon their limbs—the base of the arms (*aṅge bāhvoḥ mūle*)—the two purifiers, the lotus and the discus (*pavitre abja-cakre*); that is to say, they install them. As for others, the ancient ones (*purāṇāḥ purātanāḥ*), in response to the inquiry as to how many marks (*liṅgāni*) they place on their limbs, the meaning is: "as many as all Your marks are, so many they place."

They offer or cast [it]. Here, because the discus is presented as being inherent in Śrī Viṣṇu, it becomes established as the discus in its form as a deity. By the two words *carṣaṇīndra* and *purāṇa*, the connection with the time of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is indicated. Thus, since the mantra presents the deity of the discus connected to the time of installation, its suitability for application (*viniyoga*) in the ritual at hand is established.

Alternatively, the consistency of the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* with the present context is possible precisely because they reveal Viṣṇu himself. Here, indeed, it is described that certain leaders of men (*carṣaṇīndrāḥ*), who are full of knowledge, place upon the base of their arms Your two purifiers, O Viṣṇu—the lotus and the discus—in order to cross the ocean of birth; others, the ancient seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*), apply those heated five weapons to their limbs, bodies. Through such descriptions as "heated oceans" and so forth, the meaning is expressed; therein, the manifestation of the discus in its divine form is accomplished.

That [interpretation] is indeed inconsistent with the context; for a discus and so forth, which are marks to be worn by a person, do not pertain to the ritual action under discussion. Therefore, the meaning of "taptacakrādi" [as interpreted by you] is simply unacceptable; rather, a meaning must be described that is consistent with its application to the subject at hand. Consequently, the injunction for branding with the heated discus is not established on the strength of the scriptural citations adduced from the Pañcarātra.

Even so, it is said: "Having heated the discus (*cakra*) in fire, one should place it on the right arm of a non-Brāhmaṇa; having heated the conch (*śaṅkha*) in fire, one should place it on the left arm of a non-Brāhmaṇa. The exponents of the Veda say: 'Then, by means of these two origins—the Sudarśana marked upon the arm and the conch—those Brāhmaṇas who are desirous of heaven go to the celestial realm, and they extend the creation of the mortal world. Having taken up the conch and the discus of Viṣṇu, and having utterly burnt away Nirṛti with the well-heated discus."

If it is argued that the injunction for branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*) is indeed established by the *Kaivalya-śruti*, which says, "And he who goes beyond death," and by the *Atharvaṇa-śruti*, which says, "The hotr’s staff together with the fire, and the *pāñcajanya* discus, are heated and worn on the two arms; one should perform what is beneficial to the Self; one should offer this properly to the Teacher; therefore one becomes Vaikuṇṭha, there is no returning again, and having sacrificed, one attains the same world"—then [we reply]: No, because this has not been mentioned by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*, such as Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba, Bhāradvāja, and Kātyāyana.

This is because neither the authors of the *Karmamīmāṃsā*, such as Jaimini, nor the authors of the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*, such as Vyāsa, have cited it anywhere—whether in Śrauta or Smārta rites—for the purpose of application (*viniyoga*) or for the determination of meaning; and even though it is cited in non-Vedic systems like the *Pāñcarātra*, its status as Śruti cannot be determined by that alone by those who follow the Veda. Otherwise, one would also have to determine the Śrauta status of the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other doctrines propounded in those very same scriptures.

Otherwise, there would result the inconsistency of the sūtras beginning with "Because of the impossibility of origination" (BS 2.2.42) establishing the lack of authority for those [Pāñcarātra] āgamas composed by Vyāsa; and there would also result the inconsistency of the prescription of penance for one marked with a heated disc in the Dharmaśāstras.

As for the attempt to demonstrate that those scriptural statements which establish the rule of branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*) as pertaining only to *śūdras* are outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*), that very argument reveals its own [inconsistency]. For the statement, "Therefore, a *śūdra* alone should wear the conch and discus on his two arms," has been cited by the authors of the Dharmaśāstras and Nibandhas as being of established Vedic origin; furthermore, it is more authoritative because it contains the restrictive particle *eva*, which excludes others. It is therefore more appropriate to infer an unestablished Śruti passage in accordance with that [authoritative citation] rather than the other way around.

It is appropriate to say that the word "Brāhmaṇa" found in the Vedic passage beginning with "Taking the wheel, having heated it in fire," etc., refers to the Śūdra by taking it as denoting the quality of preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya-guṇa*), just as the word "fire" in the sentence "This boy is fire" refers to the boy [Māṇavaka]. Otherwise, if it were taken as referring to the caste (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇahood, then—just like the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice and other such rites—the injunction would pertain exclusively to Brāhmaṇas; this would result in a contradiction with experience, since the practice of those [rites] is observed even among Śūdras.

Furthermore, it would result in the inconsistency of the teachings in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts, which establish that for one who has fallen away from the *śrauta* and *smārta* rites, there is indeed a rule for such restoration (*tad-vidhi*). Likewise, the injunctions in the *Dharmaśāstras* regarding the re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*) of a Brāhmaṇa marked with the heated conch and discus, the prescription of a six-year *kṛcchra* penance, and the prescription of penance for one who sees or touches such a Brāhmaṇa would be inconsistent [if the term were not used in this sense]. Alternatively, even if the term refers to the caste (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇahood, there is no logical inconsistency.

"Therefore, one who is a *śūdra* alone should wear the conch and discus with two arms. In this passage, the word *śūdra* is accepted as referring to one who is ineligible for ritual action (*karmānadhikārī*). This is because such usage is seen in texts like: "One becomes a *śūdra* by birth; one becomes twice-born (*dvija*) by ritual actions," and so forth. Thus, according to the analogy of the "animal and the goat" (*paśucchāganyāya*), the injunction for branding with the heated discus is obtained as applying specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who is ineligible for Śrauta and Smārta rituals. And so, the exposition in the Dharmaśāstras establishes that this injunction applies only to one who is devoid of Śrauta and Smārta ritual duties.

This text covers the demonstration of the loss of caste (*pātitya*) when branding is performed by a Brāhmaṇa authorized for ritual acts; the prescription of re-initiation (*saṃskāra*) for one who has been branded; the prescription of the six-year *kṛcchra* penance; and likewise, the prescription of penances for seeing, touching, or conversing with such a person. Thus, this very statement reveals its own status as being outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*), thereby clarifying that those who maintain the branding of the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*) pertains only to Śūdras.

Rather than accepting that the great sages such as Vedavyāsa and others—who were born from portions of the Lord, who established the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, who composed the great compendia of Dharmaśāstra, and who were the authors of the Kalpasūtras including Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba, and Baudhāyana—are outside the Veda, it is more appropriate to abandon the status of "Śruti" for those [texts] whose Vedic nature is subject to doubt; for even while accepting those [doubtful] Śrutis, it is possible to provide a justification according to the method already stated.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the logic of the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, the word "Śūdra" could refer to a Brāhmaṇa through the etymological derivation "one who runs away from grief" (*śucād udvrajet*); for in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that a Śūdra might possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) because the word "Śūdra" is heard in reference to Jānaśruti, [the sūtra] concludes that since the knowledge of Brahman is preceded by the study of the Veda, and since eligibility for the Veda is possible only for those castes eligible for initiation (*upanayana*), there is no possibility of a Śūdra—who is not eligible for initiation—studying the Veda.

Because [the status of] being a Brahmin preceded by [Vedic study] is impossible for him, it was stated that the term "Śūdra" applied to Jānaśruti is etymological (based on his character). However, in this case, since the branding with the heated discus does not presuppose Vedic study, it is possible even for a Śūdra who has not undergone initiation (*upanayana*); thus, the logic of the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the exclusion of Śūdras) does not apply here. If it is argued: "Nevertheless, since injunctions regarding the branding with the conch and discus are found in the *Hārīta-smṛti* and other texts, such branding must indeed be Vedic," we say no. This is because those texts have not been cited by the authors of the digests on Dharmaśāstra, and thus they are tainted by the suspicion of being later interpolations.

Because it is impossible to ascertain their authority, and because they are contradicted by the citations of Viṣṇu, Gobhila, Śātātapa, Marīci, Manu, Bodhāyana, and others from the *Smṛtis* provided by the authors of Dharmaśāstra compendia such as Vaidyanātha and Hemādri, as well as by numerous statements from the *Purāṇas*—including the *Brahma*, *Kaurma*, *Mānava*, *Nāradīya*, *Vāyu*, *Liṅga*, *Vahni*, Āditya, Parāśara, and other Purāṇas—and because, according to the maxim that "that which is more extensive is stronger," these [latter sources] must be accepted while those [former ones] are not to be relied upon.

Nor should it be argued that there is an option between acceptance and non-acceptance due to their being of equal strength; for the statement "whatever Manu said is medicine" establishes his authority as understood from scripture, and thus an equality of strength is not established because of the contradiction with the words of Manu. Indeed, the preeminence of Manu is remembered because he was the compiler of the meaning of the Vedas: "But that Smṛti which is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not praised. That unsurpassed Dharmaśāstra which was proclaimed by Manu in the past—one should not transgress that word if one desires one's own welfare."

Furthermore, since the lack of authority for those [texts] that contradict the words of Manu has been determined by the statements of Bṛhaspati, Aṅgiras, and others cited in the *Smṛticandrikā*, even the suspicion of equal force (*samabalakatva*) does not arise. Therefore, one should conclude that the practice is indeed non-Vedic—just as the desire to cross the ocean with a raft made from the hollow of a bamboo is futile—and instead live at ease, having accepted its non-Vedic nature, rather than attempting to justify its Vedic character through the words of Hārīta and others whose authenticity is marred by the suspicion of being fabricated, or through similar scriptural passages that act like a leaky boat.

Therefore, the branding with heated discs is a matter pertaining solely to those outside the Vedic fold; it must be avoided from afar by all followers of the Vedas at all times, and it should never be respected even in thought under any circumstances—enough said.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Garuḍācalayajvan, the crest-jewel among scholars residing on the illustrious Veṅkaṭagiri, and the Kaustubha gem of the ocean of the Śrī Velu Veṃṭi lineage.
The work entitled *Taptacakrāṅkana-vidhvaṃsana* (The Refutation of the Branding with Heated Discs) is completed.
Oṃ tat sat.
